The MINERvA detector is a fine-grained hydrocarbon scintillator tracker upstream of the MINOS near detector.
The NuMI beam at Fermilab provided an average antineutrino energy of 6 GeV for this measurement.
Neutrons are detected via inelastic scattering producing recoil protons or de-excitation photons visible as isolated charge deposits.
Neutron candidates must deposit at least 1.5 MeV of energy and be within 1.5 m of the interaction vertex.
The measurement focuses on events with two or more neutrons and visible hadronic energy (available energy) less than 100 MeV.
The neutron detection efficiency for neutrons with kinetic energy between 10 and 50 MeV is nearly 50%.
GENIE 2.12.6 with the Valencia 2p2h model and MnvTunev1 empirical tune was used for simulation.
The cross section is extracted differentially as a function of muon transverse momentum.
The selected event sample has 39% efficiency and 39% purity, with 299,182 interactions selected in data.
Backgrounds include single-neutron CCQE interactions and events with mis-reconstructed available energy, often involving pions.
Simulations over-predict the rate of neutron candidates with less than 10 MeV energy deposit.
The neutron reconstruction algorithm excludes charge deposits near the vertex to reduce contamination from charged hadrons.
Muon momentum cuts require muons to have momentum between 2 and 20 GeV/c and angle less than 20 degrees relative to the beam.
The cross section measurement disagrees with several leading neutrino interaction models, indicating deficiencies in neutron production modeling.
The analysis uses an unfolding procedure to correct for detector effects and backgrounds.
The measurement is relevant for constraining neutron production models in oscillation experiments such as NOvA, T2K, and DUNE.
The Valencia 2p2h model enhances the rate of two-particle two-hole interactions between CCQE and delta resonance peaks.
Final state interactions are simulated using GENIE’s hA effective single-step algorithm.
The analysis uses data-driven sidebands to constrain backgrounds and reduce model dependence.
Neutron candidates can be formed from two- or three-dimensional clusters of charge deposits in the scintillator.
